https://openalex.org/W7155221036.title: Emotional intelligence, spiritual intelligence and intrinsic motivation as predictors of leadership effectiveness: the mediating role of organisational citizenship behaviour in Indian higher education institutions
https://openalex.org/W7155221036.abstract: Purpose The present manuscript examines the relationships among emotional intelligence (EI), spiritual intelligence (SI) and intrinsic motivation (IM) as antecedent constructs. It tests the role of organisational citizenship behaviour (OCB) as a possible mediating variable in the transformation of these psychological intelligences into efficacious academic leadership. The research has also examined the effects of these variables on the effectiveness of leadership at the faculty and academic leadership levels in north Indian higher education institutions (HEIs). Grounded in the frameworks of social exchange theory (SET) and self-determination theory (SDT), the authors intend to determine whether OCB is a behavioural conduit that enables the expression of various forms of psychological intelligence to translate into effective academic leadership. Design/methodology/approach To test the proposed hypotheses, an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design is employed. Phase 1 uses a structured survey administered to 493 faculty and academic leaders across 12 institutions in Haryana. The instrument contains five validated scales: WLEIS (EI), SISRI-24 (SI), WEIMS (IM), an adapted OCB scale and an adapted leadership practices inventory (LPI). Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) based on SmartPLS 4.0 is used to quantify the data, with mediation analysed via bootstrapping (10,000 resamples). Phase 2 is semi-structured and consists of phenomenological interviews with 17 selected academic leaders, selected based on experience and position. NVivo14 enables the reflexive thematic analysis process, following the approach of Braun and Clarke (2021). Integration of qualitative and quantitative findings is achieved through a joint display with a thread strategy. Findings All six hypotheses get empirical support. EI, SI and IM predict OCB independently and significantly (R2 = 0.587). OCB is the most prominent predictor of leadership effectiveness (β(v) = 0.562, f2 = 0.389). Bootstrapped mediation analysis results show that OCB significantly mediates the relationship between EI and leadership effectiveness (indirect effect = 0.192, 95 % confidence interval (CI)**** = [0.133, 0.255]) and IM and leadership effectiveness (indirect effect = 0.154, 95% CI**** = [0.101, 0.209]). These quantitative pathways are corroborated by qualitative themes, namely, emotional attunement as leadership currency, meaning and transcendence, intrinsic drive as behavioural fuel and OCB as leadership visibility. Participants indicated that while OCB is not required, it is an expression of academic leaders' internal intelligence, enhancing credibility and fostering colleague support over time. Practical implications The study informs the design of Emotional Intelligence Development Programs (EIDPs), the development of meaning-making platforms to foster spiritual intelligence, and the development of autonomy-supportive governance structures to maintain intrinsic motivation among academic leaders. Furthermore, accreditation bodies like the National Assessment and Accreditation Council may formalise OCB as a momentum in academic performance metrics. Finally, leadership development programmes should use mixed-methods evaluation to capture both quantifiable outcomes and experiential aspects of leadership development. Originality/value The study makes three new and novel contributions. First, it integrates EI, SI and IM into a single explanatory model of leadership effectiveness. Second, it shifts the role of OCB from a dependent variable to a mediating variable and demonstrates how psychological intelligence manifests in material organisational behaviour. Third, this theoretical framework is situated within the specific cultural and institutional context of HEIs in India, thereby contributing to decolonised, contextualised leadership theories. The inclusion of culturally embedded ideas such as (action) seva (selfless service) and dharmic purpose clarifies previously unanticipated relationships between SI and OCB.

https://openalex.org/W4410291061.title: Heterogenous Impact of Leadership Styles on Employee Performance and the Mediating Role of Employee Engagement: An Empirical Study on Private SMEs in Malawi
https://openalex.org/W4410291061.abstract: In recent years, the crucial role of matching leadership styles with employee performance in the management of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) has been increasingly acknowledged in different developing countries, Malawi included. Properly adopting, a given leadership style can keep employees performing at their best, which sends a productive signal for organizational growth and sustainability. Conversely, adopting an inappropriate leadership style can often lead to a low level of motivation within employees. Thus, in general terms, performance targets are not achieved time and again due to an inability to motivate individual or groups of employees within an enterprise. However, a lot of small and medium enterprises' proprietors and managers in Malawi struggle to adopt appropriate leadership styles as they have a poor understanding of how they relate with the management of small and medium enterprises. Furthermore, there is still a lack of research in the management literature regarding the best leadership style for Malawi's SME sector. It is, therefore, imperative to identify that leadership style which best fits the management of SMEs in Malawi to heighten Employee performance. Subject to the said pressing issues, the purpose of this study is to determine the direct and indirect impact of leadership styles on the levels of performance of employees in SMEs while taking employee engagement as an interposing variable, more specifically focused on the level of democratic, autocratic, and charismatic leadership. The study will thus try to examine how each behavioral component of those three styles of leadership would function towards promoting SME performance within the Malawian economy. Thus, the study recommends that charismatic leadership style be prioritized in the SME sector to enhance Employee performance. It is also suggested that a comprehensive leaders' training program, organized by recognized institutions, be introduced to enhance the level of Democratic and Autocratic leadership skills among SME entrepreneurs in Malawi. This paper scrutinized leadership styles impact on performance levels of employees in SMEs with employee engagement as the mediating variable. Three hundred questionnaires were distributed, and data from 231 employees from various private small and medium enterprises in Malawi were collected. SPSS was used to process and measure the analysis and structural models. Using a cross-sectional survey design, data was collected from 231 employees from various private SMEs, with subsequent analysis using structural equation modeling to explore direct and indirect effects. The results indicate that charismatic leadership had the strongest positive impact on both employee engagement and performance, followed by democratic and autocratic leadership styles. Charismatic leadership was particularly effective in fostering an emotionally engaging work environment that promoted both higher performance and motivation. Democratic leadership also significantly enhanced engagement and performance by fostering inclusivity in decision-making processes. Interestingly, autocratic leadership, although traditionally seen as limiting autonomy, positively impacted employee performance by providing structure and clarity. Employee engagement was found to mediate the relationship between all three leadership styles and employee performance, emphasizing its critical role in translating effective leadership into productive outcomes. The study concludes that adaptive leadership styles, tailored to specific organizational contexts, can significantly enhance employee engagement and performance, providing actionable insights for leaders in Malawi’s SME sector. One of the key variables in determining how engaged employees are with their leader, the company, and the company's success is their leadership style. So far, there have been studies on the relationship between leadership style, employee performance, and employee engagement at the district level. However, there has yet to be research on the relationship between leadership style, employee performance, and the engagement of employees in the private sector in Malawi, which is a gap that needs to be researched. Therefore, this study examines the relationship between three leadership styles, namely Autocratic leadership, charismatic leadership, and Democratic leadership, concerning engagement in work and performance of private sector employees.

https://openalex.org/W2897854788.title: Ophthalmology training and teaching in India: How these young ophthalmologists can become leaders of tomorrow?
https://openalex.org/W2897854788.abstract: Sir, The editor and editorial board of Indian Journal of Ophthalmology deserve applause for publishing excellent editorial/articles in the June issue of IJO. Residency training is one of the crucial phases in a doctor's life which transforms a theoretical generalist to a practical specialist geared up to take on the responsibility of caring for patients. Ophthalmology offers the adrenalin rush associated with performing delicate sight-restoring surgeries, yet the eye specialists do not deal with stressful life and death situations. Throughout the years, the surgical training process in ophthalmology has progressed from unstructured apprenticeship to limitless period in the past, and then in the 20th century shifted to a Halstedian pyramidal structure and currently on consistent rectangular model with specified timeline.[1] However, the “See one, do one, teach one” concept of the Halstedian model is still ingrained in the residency. Several authors emphasized that ophthalmology residency training in India still needs to be improved significantly.[234] Without proper and updated residency training system in a majority of medical colleges in India, how would young ophthalmologists become the leaders in their field? In India, 60% residency training for ophthalmology is under government-run organizations while the remaining are private institutions.[5] The imparted training is typically done in various settings such as medical colleges (including regional institutes) and private institutes. There is not a coherent training system followed by all which leads to huge variations in quality of training. It is important to ensure that residents in India observe (and perform under supervision, if possible) a good variety of ophthalmic surgeries. The shortage of standardization shows the need for a stronger regulatory authority to make these changes and implement them efficiently.[67] It is important to have such a training system which focuses on the actuality of the learning process, human resources, and the infrastructure. In addition, the training system must be need-based. Standards must be established and followed. There is a dire need to emphasize the residents’ role as researches and teachers throughout their residency to encourage them to become leaders.[8] This is one of the major parts of competency-based curriculum for residency training of young ophthalmologists around the globe.[9] There is a strong need for the authorities to do major rethinking and correction in the curriculum and training system.[10] Numerous ophthalmologists have stressed the need of establishing a fresh training system for the residency students in ophthalmology.[11] Moreover, it has been stressed that the potential of young ophthalmologists of India must be encouraged to take the leadership role. This can be done if the residency students have a great foundation of teaching and training. Two examples deserve special mention here: I-Focus, National Postgraduate Education Programme in Ophthalmology and Academic and Research Committee (ARC) wing of All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS), both have done commendable work to update residents in basic and cutting-edge ophthalmology and helped them to prepare for leadership role. Residents in training would play a major role in shaping up in to the future leaders of ophthalmology, if they have all the essential elements – patient care, skill-based practice, practice-based improvement, and learning, professionalism, communication, and interpersonal skills leading to their continuous professional development.[12] The training system must provide them a chance for open-minded learning of comprehensive ophthalmology and a broad-based approach. It is up to the coordinators of residency training and ophthalmology heads of various institutions to come up with the will to make these changes and also to lead this change throughout ophthalmology in India. There are numerous ways these changes can happen – a teaching schedule, one-on-one mentorship for residents, encourage young ophthalmologist to teach, management of their time, and reorganization in the departments. There are numerous ways through which these young ophthalmologists can become leaders of tomorrow. First, it is essential for them to find the right mentor, someone who is genuinely interested in helping them adapt leadership qualities instead of someone who hardly offers any useful advice. Most importantly, they have to actually listen to their mentors, even if it is a hard feedback. Moreover, young ophthalmologists need to become more proactive if they truly want to become future leaders.[13] There is no point in waiting for someone to hand them the responsibilities; they need to show their mentors and leaders that they have what it takes to be in a leadership role. These future leaders should also be engaged in member ophthalmic organizations and participation in national and international ophthalmic conferences right from the initial stage.[14] Another important thing these young ophthalmologists must consider is stepping out of their comfort zone. They must trust their education and training and must not be afraid to learn new technique and skill that can open more opportunities for them to move on to leadership roles.[15] It is essential to keep in mind that these young ophthalmologists are the future of ophthalmology. Using innovative teaching styles and techniques to help today's technically driven residents to learn more efficiently. We admire sincere efforts of Dr. Santosh G. Honavar and the entire editorial team of Indian Journal of Ophthalmology for publishing valuable suggestions that are needed to be taken to make immediate changes in training and teaching in ophthalmology residency to ensure a bright and prosperous future of ophthalmology in India. Financial support and sponsorship Nil. Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts of interest.

https://openalex.org/W2066948558.title: The Suspension of Treatments in ADAPT: Concerns beyond the Cardiovascular Safety of Celecoxib or Naproxen
https://openalex.org/W2066948558.abstract:
Dr. Nissen's comments [1] on our paper [2] reveal a fundamental difference in his and our perspectives on the ethical conduct of clinical trials. While we agree with his central point that the ADAPT data do not permit definitive conclusions regarding the safety of naproxen or celecoxib, we doubt Dr. Nissen's conjecture that the ADAPT safety data could—or should—have been more interpretable had a different model of data review been applied to adverse events.

Safety data in ADAPT, as in most trials, were not collected to test hypotheses. Instead, they were collected to protect trial subjects from harm to the extent possible, and to ensure that the investigators and the funding agency fulfilled their important obligations on this point. Stopping a trial for benefit and stopping to avoid harm are, fortunately, not symmetrical occurrences: typically one stops to avoid harm when inference is far less certain than would be required to affirm benefit. This principle—a direct reflection of the trial investigator's ethical obligations to study participants—was especially important for ADAPT, a primary prevention trial with 7–10 years of planned interventions and no anticipated short-term benefits. For the same reason, the stopping rules mentioned by Dr. Nissen are typically applied to prevent a premature conclusion of benefit, not of harm.

To clarify, it was the ADAPT Steering Committee, and not the National Institutes of Health (NIH), that bore ultimate responsibility for the decision to suspend the ADAPT treatments. The suspension of celecoxib was a direct consequence of Pfizer's announcement on December 17, 2004, of termination of the APC and PreSAP trials, citing cardiovascular risks with celecoxib [3] even though, as our paper shows, the ADAPT data suggested little cardiovascular risk with celecoxib [2].

The decision to suspend treatment with naproxen was more difficult. As we told the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Advisory Committee [4], the safety data “…. would not in themselves have led to a decision to suspend either treatment…[because of any] conclusion that this signal [with naproxen] was…sufficiently compelling or definitive to warrant a recommendation to suspend the treatment.” Yet, several operational issues would have made continuation of the naproxen arm difficult. These included a necessity to obtain revised consent from participants—hence, review of new consent forms by seven Institutional Review Boards—as well as a reluctance to imply, by continuing naproxen, that it was “safe” while celecoxib was not.

Both decisions were taken in consultation with the Chair of the trial's data monitoring committee and with program staff of the National Institute on Aging. But in any event, on December 23, six days later, the FDA put a Full Clinical Hold on ADAPT and other primary prevention trials that administered celecoxib. The procedures required for reinstatement of the ADAPT investigational new drug (IND) application would have taken months, and in the interim all treatments would have been suspended regardless of our earlier decision.

We concur with Dr. Nissen, nonetheless, about the lamentable and somewhat misleading publicity that surrounded our decision. On December 20, 2004, the NIH Director's office reviewed the preliminary ADAPT cardiovascular safety results and forwarded them to the leadership of the FDA. The NIH Deputy Director then convened a conference call with the ADAPT Study Chair (JCSB) and Director of the Coordinating Center (CLM) to announce that a press teleconference would be held in cooperation with the FDA later that day. While that press conference was in process, the Director's office issued the press release referenced by Dr. Nissen, after which the ADAPT Study Chair was asked to answer several reporters' questions. The ensuing press coverage is well summarized by Dr. Nissen.

We also lament the long delay in publication of the ADAPT cardiovascular safety results. In fact, with full acknowledgement of their limitations, we had submitted these results to no fewer than five other journals before they were accepted by PLoS Clinical Trials. Consistently, the reason for rejection was that the data were “not definitive” (as we had acknowledged) or that results ran counter to expectation. Notwithstanding the logistical difficulties cited, we were surprised to learn of the other journals' evident view that publication of the ADAPT safety results would have been justified only if the treatments had been continued until there was a clear demonstration of harm with naproxen.

We remain resolute in our convictions on the following principles:

1. Ultimately, it is the investigators who are responsible for the well-being of those studied in trials. They report to Institutional Review Boards; data monitoring committees do not.

2. One does not do trials to find “significant” or “definitive” evidence of harm, especially in long-term prevention trials with healthy people. The risk–benefit balance in such trials is especially vulnerable to unforeseen situations such as arose for ADAPT on December 17, 2004.

3. Before blaming anyone for the decision to suspend treatments in ADAPT, one should consider the “mother test.” Given what is now known, would you have advised your aging mother to remain a participant receiving treatments in ADAPT? No member of the ADAPT leadership could answer this question “yes.”

4. While almost all will agree that some data—especially those from a randomized experiment unlikely to be repeated—are better than none, most journal editors and reviewers seem paradoxically to prefer “significant” or “definitive” untoward results. We think this is unfortunate. We agree that these data should have been published long ago. We are grateful to the editors of PLoS Clinical Trials for taking us at our word and publishing them.

https://openalex.org/W4286559490.title: HRSA's Investment in Public Health Training Centers
https://openalex.org/W4286559490.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has demonstrated the relevance, importance, and value of the nation's public health workforce. Although not as easily defined or demarcated as other health professions, public health is a critical health workforce specialty, just as primary care physicians, nurses, dentists, and other health professions whose training is supported by the Health Resources and Service Administration's (HRSA's) Bureau of Health Workforce. Comprising both the Preventive Medicine Residency program and the Public Health Training Centers (PHTCs), the Bureau's public health workforce portfolio, although relatively small, is a unique and critical component of the federal government's overall public health efforts. A previous supplement in the Journal of Public Health Management and Practice discussed the activities of the Preventive Medicine Residency program.1 In this volume, we focus on the PHTCs and their role in training the US public health workforce. Public Health Training Unlike most health professions supported by HRSA's Bureau of Health Workforce programs, the PHTC program is unique because of the field that it supports. There is no singular career path into the field of public health. Since there is no standardized career pathway for those entering public health, there is no standard training curriculum required for entry into the field. Unlike nursing, dentistry, or medicine, there is no limitation on who can enter the public health workforce at most levels (although some jurisdictions may require a physician to lead their health departments). Still, public health can be defined as a unique profession. As stated in a seminal treatise on public health education, “The ordinary medical training does not qualify a person to be a health officer any more than the training suitable for public health service would qualify a man to practice medicine.”2(p794) Although public health may be a unique body of study, the 2017 Public Health Workforce Interests and Needs Survey (PH WINS) found that only 14% of the public health workforce has formal degrees in public health.3 And although formal training in the science of public health may include the core disciplines of epidemiology and biostatistics, environmental and behavioral health, and health policy and management, survey respondents still believed public health workers needed training in budgeting and financial management, systems and strategic thinking, and change management and developing a vision for a healthy community. The Art of Public Health Just as there is an art to direct clinical care, we must acknowledge that there is an art to public health. Akin to the “bedside manner” of clinicians, the art consists of a set of skills for the public health practitioner that transcends the science of public health and has significant implications in the success of the practitioner. If the art of clinical care can be summarized as using soft skills of communication and persuasion to achieve health outcomes in patients, the art of public health could be considered soft skills such as sound management and problem solving, which are essential to the health of populations. In fact, if effective bedside manner requires a deep understanding of the patient, the same can be said of public health and an understanding of the community to be served. The beginnings of formal public health education in the 20th century acknowledged the same: “With these points in view, the next matter requiring our attention is that since the education is to be for service, it must be practical, but a practical art based on sound science.”2(p794) Even the Welch-Rose report indicated in its requirements for modern public health education, The mere assembling of such courses does not constitute a school of hygiene. The great need of the country today ... is the establishment of well equipped and adequately supported institutes or laboratories of hygiene, where ... opportunities are afforded for thorough training in both the science and the art.4(p6) The Bureau's experience with health professional training shows that the most effective training occurs with the patients to be served: if we expect clinicians to succeed in rural areas or with underserved populations, their training should take place in the same areas. Public health training should be no exception. And thus, the PHTCs endeavor to provide practical training within communities with public health needs. Training the Public Health Workforce The PHTC program began in 1999 to support the accreditation movement among local health departments and the defining of competencies among public health workers. The program has changed to meet public health needs over the ensuing 2 decades. Just as the PHTCs' transformation in 2013 allowed them to provide rapid response training during the 2014 Ebola crisis,5 the program has an opportunity now to address public health workforce needs that have been exposed in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. To provide a flavor of HRSA-funded PHTCs' activities, during academic year 2019-2020, PHTCs oversaw experiential field placements at 278 sites across 48 states and Puerto Rico, which included state, local, and tribal health departments, Federally Qualified Health Centers and community health centers, hospitals, community-based organizations, and other settings; 74% of sites were located in medically underserved communities, 29% were in primary care settings, and 26% were in rural areas. In addition, PHTCs provided 2779 continuing education courses that reached 307 750 individuals, a quarter of whom worked in medically underserved communities. The projects collected in this supplement demonstrate the wide range of training activities funded through the HRSA-funded PHTCs: from an overview of PHTCs as a partner in workforce development to assessments of adaptive leadership and various modes of training; from systems thinking and issues in equity to an evaluation of a national pilot and an appraisal of COVID-19 activities across the PHTCs. The PHTCs are dynamic and spirited hubs of programmatic activity, looking to match the present and future needs of the public health workforce. In 1991, HRSA's then-Administrator Robert Harmon wrote of HRSA's role in public health, “It is essential that HRSA identify major weaknesses in the system and assist in correcting them.” He continued, “Filling the gaps in health care infrastructure ... is a responsibility unique to HRSA.”6(p7) We, the authors, agree wholeheartedly, and it is with this charge that we look toward future iterations of the PHTC program. Future Directions of the Public Health Training Centers After more than 20 years, the PHTCs remain a vibrant and vital program dedicated to training a public health workforce responsive to the needs of the nation. The need for a strong public health workforce will continue past the COVID-19 pandemic, and HRSA's PHTC program will continue to evolve and adapt to the needs of the workforce, keeping the art of the practice at the forefront of our training goals.

https://openalex.org/W7130819150.title: Competency-based Medical Education in India: Between Promise and Practice
https://openalex.org/W7130819150.abstract: When the National Medical Commission (formerly Medical Council of India) rolled out the Competency-based Medical Education (CBME) curriculum in 2019, it signaled a decisive shift from time-bound, knowledge-heavy training to outcomes that define the Indian Medical Graduate as clinician, communicator, leader, professional, and lifelong learner.[1] In spirit, the reform is contextual and ambitious; in practice, its implementation has been uneven – producing notable innovations, visible friction, and systemic gaps that continue to test institutions across the country. The Arc of Change: Why Competency-based Medical Education Matters CBME’s merit lies in its clarity of purpose: articulate competencies, scaffold learning with Early Clinical Exposure (ECE), integration across disciplines, Attitude, Ethics, and Communication (AETCOM), and strengthened formative and summative assessments.[1] The rationale was compelling – addressing trust deficits in health care, aligning training with societal needs, and moving beyond rote learning to entrustable capabilities in real settings.[1,2] Yet, translating this vision into everyday timetables, lesson plans, and assessment rubrics has required colleges to reengineer processes, retool faculty, and reinvest in infrastructure. Successes Worth Noting ECE and integration have gained traction. Reports from multiple institutions describe positive student perceptions of ECE, small-group learning, and horizontal/vertical integration that connect basic, paraclinical, and clinical strands. Students consistently find integrated teaching beneficial, and many value case-based learning, Demonstrate, Observe, Assist, Perform sessions, and reflective practices embedded in CBME.[3,4] AETCOM is gaining legitimacy. Implementation studies suggest that phased AETCOM instruction – supported by role-play, panel discussions, and problem-oriented approaches – improves knowledge scores and is well-received.[5,6] Faculty development has scaled up. The revised basic course workshop, ACME, and Curriculum Implementation Support Program (CISP) have catalyzed a national training effort. While the depth varies, departments are increasingly using departmental planners, structured lesson plans, logbooks, and varied assessment tools aligned to competencies.[2,7] Programmatic clarity is improving. Frameworks for integration and templates for implementing newer components (Foundation Course, ECE, Electives, and Clerkship) have been disseminated, offering practical anchors to the faculty new to CBME.[3,8] Implementation Barriers: Frictions and Systemic Challenges Despite these gains, implementation barriers recur across studies and college experiences. Overload without orchestration The extensive list of competencies (>2500) interacts with rigid timetables and uneven interdepartmental coordination. Faculty encounter difficulty with precise objective framing, avoiding content overlap, and aligning teaching–learning with assessments at scale.[7,8] Assessment inconsistencies Although CBME prescribes robust feedback, workplace-based assessments, and logbook tracking, standardization remains inconsistent. Logbooks often become perfunctory, and student understanding of new assessment schemes varies widely.[4,7] Faculty readiness and bandwidth Surveys reveal limited awareness of CBME-aligned faculty development programs, increased workload, and insufficient training in self-directed learning (SDL) facilitation, simulation teaching, and programmatic assessment.[7,9] Institutional readiness varies widely, creating inequities in skill-lab and e-learning access. A multicentric study suggests that many faculty display a “non-user” profile toward CBME, indicating the need for training beyond CISP.[10] Infrastructure and resource deficit CBME assumes access to functional skill labs, simulation facilities, and standardized patients – resources unevenly distributed across colleges, especially those with rapidly expanding intakes.[7,8] Curriculum governance and coordination gaps Phase coordination, committee functioning, and integration mapping are inconsistent. Without coherent leadership, integration risks becoming episodic.[7] Cultural adoption among clinicians Clinicians under service pressure may resist additional educational responsibilities, limiting workplace-based assessments and EPA use. Specialty commentaries highlight structural and cultural barriers to sustained adoption.[2] Attitude, ethics, and communication fidelity and assessment While AETCOM is widely welcomed, several reviews emphasize that success depends on faculty capacity, appropriate assessment mix (Objective-structured clinical examination, mini-clinical examination, reflective writing), and institutional support for longitudinal mentorship – areas still evolving.[2,5,6] Student workload and wellbeing Although CBME aspires to learner – centricity, Phase I students frequently report academic stress and insufficient time for physical activity – suggesting that well-being requires explicit protection.[4] What Has Worked: Features to Retain Integrated, small-group teaching consistently improves student engagement and perceived learning quality.[3,4] Colleges that operationalize structured timetables, clear departmental lesson plans, and alignment integration maps report smoother rollouts and fewer clashes.[3,7] Similarly, hybrid problem-oriented approaches to AETCOM (combining sensitization, SDL, role-plays, and panel discussions) show measurable gains in knowledge and case closure performance.[5] These are low-cost, high-yield strategies that should be mainstreamed across phases. What Must Change: From Compliance to Capability Colleges should prepare local competency maps that prioritize context – relevant “must-do” skills while meeting national minima. Periodic reviews – incorporating student and clinician feedback – can declutter overlaps and protect time for skills practice.[1,7] Assessment literacy must become a core institutional strength. Training in blueprinting, standard - setting, reliability, and constructive feedback is essential.[2,7,9] Clinician educators require structural support, recognition of teaching effort in appraisal, protected time, and alignment of service and educational quality indicators.[2] Specialty commentaries warn that clinician resistance is partly structural; aligning incentives will reduce friction and improve workplace assessment adoption.[2] Priorities for the Next Phase of Competency-based Medical Education Recent editorials and updates suggest that the 2024 revisions to the CBME curriculum have raised the stakes further – prompting reflections that implementation remains “more of a challenge than an opportunity” in some settings. While such commentaries are cautionary, they reinforce the need for adaptive leadership, realistic pacing, and context-sensitive regulation that allows innovation without diluting standards.[7,11] The paradox is familiar to medical educators: CBME is both the solution and a source of new work. It demands clarity (what must every graduate do?), consistency (how will we judge it?), and courage (what will we stop doing to make room for practice and feedback?). India’s medical colleges have proven that progress is possible – ECE is happening, AETCOM is improving, and integration is visible. To accelerate momentum, India needs a deliberate shift from implementation to impact. Three priorities stand out: Strengthen assessment quality Standardized, reliable workplace-based assessments and meaningful feedback loops must become non-negotiable. Regulators should offer clearer templates, exemplars, and faculty certification pathways. Enable and empower faculty Institutions must invest in continuous faculty development, protect teaching time, and recognize educational contributions in career progression. Ensure infrastructure realism Scaling CBME requires minimum standards for skill labs, simulation spaces, and digital platforms – especially for newer and resource-limited colleges. A Call to Action A multipronged strategy, involving all stakeholders, is more likely to succeed. Regulators Regulators must provide phased, realistic guidelines; benchmark quality and support capacity building. Institutions Institutions should strengthen governance, create local competency maps, and invest in infrastructure and faculty development. Faculty Faculty should embrace educational roles, engage in assessment literacy, and model AETCOM competencies. If these priorities are pursued with coherence and commitment, CBME can fulfill its promise – not only producing competent graduates but restoring confidence in medical education as a system that learns, adapts, and serves.

https://openalex.org/W2770613463.title: Cross-Sector Collaboration for Public Innovation
https://openalex.org/W2770613463.abstract: Jacob Torfing wrote Collaborative Innovation in the Public Sector for both scholars and practitioners in the field of public administration and policy. In the book, he ambitiously aims to develop an integrative framework to explore how network-based collaboration between state and nonstate stakeholders generates innovation “by combining theoretical and empirical insights in systematically analyzing the key aspects of the processes of collaboration innovation” (p. 13). Public innovation refers to “an intended but inherently contingent process that involves the development and realization, and frequently also the spread, of new and creative ideas that challenge conventional wisdom and disrupt the established practices within a specific context” (p. 30). To help further understand innovation conceptually, Torfing suggests seven types of innovation related to public administration and policy: product innovation (newly developed products to meet citizens’ unmet needs), service innovation (new forms of public service or new ways of service delivery), process innovation (novel processes for producing public service), organizational innovation (new forms and ways of organizing public organizations), governance innovation (new modes of governing collaboration between public organizations and external stakeholders), policy innovation (novel policy tools and assessment tools), and discourse innovation (new languages and symbols to identify social problems or to change the image of public organizations). Most importantly, Torfing suggests a theory of collaborative innovation. To develop this analytical model of collaborative innovation, he reviews and combines a wide range of theoretical and empirical insights from innovation theory, theories of network governance, institutional theory, systems and complexity theory, theories of learning, and discourse theory. The analytical model consists of five key dimensions: initial conditions, institutional arenas of interaction, public innovation outputs, evaluation of outcomes, and metagovernance. First, he takes into consideration three levels (macro, meso, and micro) of initial conditions. The macro-level conditions include “different traditions for stakeholder involvement in different countries and in different parts of the public sector” (p. 106). At the meso level, collaborative innovation is influenced by “different legal and institutional conditions for participatory governance in different policy fields” (p. 106). The micro-level conditions indicate asymmetries of power, resource and knowledge, past experiences with cooperation or conflict, and incentives for participation (Ansell and Gash 2008). As a main component of collaborative innovation theory, institutional arenas of interaction consist of three subcomponents: triggers of collaborative innovation, collaborative innovation processes, and drivers and barriers. Torfing suggests push or pull factors as the triggers of collaborative collaboration. Push factors pertain to a situation where state and nonstate stakeholders “seek to escape the present predicament, or … that is perceived to be unsustainable due to the emergence or aggravation of some serious problems” (p. 113). Pull factors are at work when state and nonstate stakeholders face positive and ambitious challenges that urge them to pursue a new and attractive direction or when we exploit new opportunities generating new and desirable things. But he notes that those pull or push factors act as “a necessary but insufficient condition for initiating public innovation processes” (p. 117). He focuses on the role of social and political entrepreneurs who problematize existing practices and construct new opportunities to develop innovative solutions. Next, Torfing conducts in-depth analysis on the different aspects of collaborative innovation processes. First, he categorizes actors of collaborative innovation processes into three types: the affected actors (those who are directly influenced by particular problems and solutions for the problems); relevant actors (those who have experience, knowledge, expertise in creating, implementing, and diffusing novel solutions); and intermediaries and boundary spanners (those who are capable of facilitating actors to share their expertise, skills, and resources with others). Mobilizing and empowering actors who have diverse and applicable assets is essential for designing and implementing innovative solutions in an institutional arena of interaction. Torfing views collaborative innovation processes as collective learning. Innovative solutions “are usually a product of learning that is stimulated by the exchange of information, views, and ideas between multiple actors with different knowledge bases and forms of expertise” (p. 180). Collaborative learning can be achieved through collective discourse by comparing and assessing the reflections of multiple actors. Especially, he introduces emerging literature on user-driven or citizen-centered innovation. From this perspective, citizens’ experiences and ideas are an important resource for producing novel public solutions. Thus, citizens are considered as proactive co-creators of innovative solutions instead of passive customers of public service. He also identifies and describes key obstacles that hinder the decision and implementation of innovative solutions. These obstacles include uncertainty about the appropriateness and impacts of solutions, probable risks, complexity caused by the involvement of multiple actors, collective action problems (prisoner’s dilemmas and free riding), and power struggles and conflicts. Torfing stresses that traditional rationalistic approaches (cost-benefit analysis and public discourse based on communicative rationality) are unlikely to address such obstacles in collaborative innovation processes. Instead, to select and implement innovative solutions, “deliberative processes must combine the accumulation of arguments based on reason with the articulation of a hegemonic discourse that is capable of mobilizing passion and constructing visions” (p. 207). Thus, he contends that conflicts and power struggles can facilitate multiple actors to pursue intelligent change in institutional arenas of interaction. Also from a practical point of view, it is important to connect the selection and implementation of innovative solutions to the daily operations of public organizations, for example, by integrating frontline personnel’s experiences and skills and competent knowledge workers’ expertise to initiate and manage collaborative innovation processes. Another important topic that needs to be considered regarding collaborative innovation processes is the diffusion of public innovation. Rogers (1995)’s innovation diffusion model consisting of five stages (knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation, and confirmation) is utilized to analyze how innovative solutions are diffused through collaborative networks. According to this model, innovation diffusion facilitates dynamic communication between suppliers of policy innovation and potential adopters and their communication “is often mediated by change agents and opinion leaders” (p. 304). Also, an organizational learning approach is emphasized to understand the impact and role of governance networks on innovation diffusion. From this perspective, innovation diffusion in governance networks is a result of a mix of the internal search for new ideas and external opportunities and knowledge. The third subcomponent of institutional arenas of interaction is drivers of and barriers to collaborative innovation in the public sector. Torfing focuses on the four types of the drivers of collaborative innovation. An important driver of innovation is problems, challenges, and opportunities identified as “public.” Those problems, challenges, and opportunities likely spur “a moral obligation to participate in processes of collaborative problem solving” (p. 239). The second driver is that public organizations are embedded in the same overall rules, norms, and values. He considers citizen engagement in policy decision making and implementation as a crucial driver of innovation. Citizen engagement oftentimes not only enables citizens to make their voices heard in the policy decision making and implementation process, but also enhances the collaborative capacity of the public sector. Torfing categorizes various barriers to collaborative innovation into three types: barriers to interaction acting as a precondition of collaboration, barriers to collaboration acting as a precondition of innovation, and barriers to innovation. The barriers to interaction include the lack of necessity or urgency regarding social problems and challenges, the absence of a tradition for interaction in the policy area, negative previous experiences with participatory and interactive decision making, and weak political support. He suggests as the barriers to collaboration large power asymmetries, a competitive environment, and opportunistic behavior. The barriers to innovation indicate the lack of diversity of worldviews, the presence of veto players blocking the group’s ability to collaborate, political complexity, and operational uncertainty. Crucially, Torfing contends that public leaders and mangers can help overcome the barriers by playing the role of conveners, facilitators, and catalysts. To address the barriers to interaction, they are required to become the convener that “brings together the relevant and affected actors and … triggers an initial exchange of information, views, and ideas” (p. 245). They also can serve as the facilitator for collaboration by managing internal differences between actors and creating mutual learning. Public leaders and managers as the catalyst need “to create appropriate disturbances and encourage the actors to think outside the box and use their different competences and capacities to develop and implement new and bold solutions” (p. 246). Torfing finally emphasizes that the roles of the convener, the facilitator, and the catalyst are based on new forms of leadership, including adaptive leadership, distributive (or horizontal) leadership, and collaborative leadership. Undoubtedly, I believe that this book and collaborative innovation theory in particular makes a significant theoretical contribution to the literature on governance networks and innovation that have been previously disconnected. Collaborative innovation theory can “help us ask some good and relevant research questions, conceptualize and categorize the main determinants in processes of collaborative innovation, and understand network-based collaboration and innovation processes” (p. 75). This book can be also useful for practitioners to understand collaborative innovation processes and to develop their own leadership and management strategies for designing and implementing innovative solutions in the public sector. However, as Torfing mentioned, collaborative innovation theory (and 41 propositions articulated in the book) calls for the further development and modification of the theory based on empirical testing. In particular, I want to emphasize two things for future research. First, collaborative innovation may not be an ultimate goal that state and nonstate stakeholders collectively pursue. In other words, multiple actors participate in designing and implementing innovative solutions to generate specific social, economic, or political benefits to individuals, organizations, or the community at large. Thus, potentially, collaborative innovation theory may need to be extended by considering its various impacts and benefits. In this regard, the public value framework can be useful (Moore 1995). This perspective takes into account a wide range of substantive (economic, political, social, strategic, and quality of life) and intrinsic (ideological and perceptional) benefits and impacts that public administration and policy can create. From this perspective, collaborative innovation may be viewed as a “value-generating mechanism” instead of a final goal and outcome (Harrison et al. 2012). Next, I note that nonstate stakeholders—including the general public, nonprofit organizations, and for-profit corporations—are currently developing and implementing collaborative innovations in diverse policy sectors (emergency preparedness and response, environmental protection, human and social services, international development, etc.). For example, in recent disaster and crisis situations, nonstate stakeholders proactively processed a large amount of disaster and crisis data from multiple sources and collaborated with government agencies to coordinate rescue missions and the delivery of aid resources in a timely and efficient manner (Park and Johnston 2017). From this perspective, nonstate stakeholders are not just “invited” collaborators. They oftentimes act as the initiators and designers of governance networks for collaborative innovation. But, it seems that collaborative innovation theory developed by Torfing focuses more attention on the role of state stakeholders than that of nonstate stakeholders. Thus, scholars may need to conduct more studies on nonstate stakeholder-driven innovation.

https://openalex.org/W4409286798.title: Reaffirming the heart of nursing
https://openalex.org/W4409286798.abstract: FigureIN RECENT YEARS, THERE has been a noticeable shift in how nurses approach their work. Although technical expertise and efficiency are critical, many of us in the profession worry that the focus on human caring has taken a back seat. Nurse leaders have observed this trend not only in students but also in literature, healthcare environments, and even among seasoned professionals.1 Nursing, at its core, has always been about caring—for people, their health, and their dignity. We need to revisit and reaffirm this foundational aspect of the profession, especially in today's fast-paced, tech-heavy healthcare system. This article explores nursing's rich history of caring, the human spirit's role in our commitment, the challenges of maintaining caring practices in a digital era, and the urgent need to keep caring central to nursing as we move further into the future. Drawing on theories and insights from leaders like Florence Nightingale, Jean Watson, Mary Eliza Mahoney, and even this author, let's reflect on what it means to truly care in today's healthcare environment. NURSING'S HISTORIC FOUNDATION IN CARING Nursing has always been rooted in caring. Florence Nightingale, often called the founder of modern nursing, set the stage with her focus on holistic care during the Crimean War. She didn't just treat wounds, she addressed patients' emotional, spiritual, and physical needs, emphasizing that compassion is as vital as clinical skills.2 Nightingale's work was grounded in a deep sense of moral duty and spiritual calling. She believed that care extended beyond mere physical treatment to include uplifting the human spirit. In the American context, Clara Barton stands out as a shining example of caring in action. Known as the “Angel of the Battlefield” during the Civil War, Barton provided comfort and medical care to soldiers, often under fire. Her actions—as well as the actions of many of the nurses in American wars—exemplified courage and selflessness, qualities that reflect the spirit of nursing. Barton later founded the American Red Cross, embedding these values into an organization that continues to prioritize humanity and compassion.3 Mary Eliza Mahoney, the first Black RN in the US, embodied the resilience and dedication central to nursing's caring spirit. Her commitment to holistic and equitable care showcased the importance of dignity and respect for every patient, regardless of race or background. Mahoney's advocacy for diversity and inclusion within the healthcare system remains a testament to the expansive nature of caring in nursing.4 Lillian Wald further deepened the legacy of nursing's caring spirit by focusing on public health. Her establishment of the Henry Street Settlement in New York City addressed the needs of underserved populations, blending medical attention with social reform. Wald believed that caring meant addressing the whole person, including their social and environmental conditions, to truly promote health and well-being.5 These historical figures and many others share a common thread: their caring wasn't limited to treating ailments but extended to advocating for justice and creating systems of support. Their work reminds us that nursing has always been about fostering hope, dignity, and connection. This caring spirit has been formalized over time into frameworks like Jean Watson's Theory of Human Caring. Although only one of many nursing theories reflecting caring, Watson's emphasis on authentic relationships and creating and leading healing environments reinforces the idea that nursing isn't just a profession but a calling to serve humanity with empathy and love.6 THE HUMAN SPIRIT IN NURSING'S COMMITMENT TO CARING Caring in nursing is both a personal and professional commitment rooted deeply in the human spirit. At its core, caring encompasses empathy, compassion, and a genuine desire to alleviate suffering. These characteristics reflect the emotional and moral dimensions of nursing that draw many individuals to the profession. Beyond skills and knowledge, caring requires attentiveness to the unique needs of each patient, recognizing their humanity and dignity. CHARACTERISTICS AND ELEMENTS OF CARING Key characteristics of caring include presence, authenticity, and responsiveness. Presence involves being fully engaged with patients, offering undivided attention, and creating a space for trust and connection.7 Authenticity ensures that nurses interact with patients honestly and openly, fostering genuine relationships. Responsiveness highlights the ability to adapt to patients' changing needs, ensuring that care remains personalized and effective. Other critical elements of caring include active listening, emotional intelligence, and advocacy. Active listening allows nurses to understand patients' concerns fully, whereas emotional intelligence helps nurses navigate complex emotions with sensitivity. Advocacy underscores the nurse's role in standing up for patients' needs and rights, especially in vulnerable situations. SPIRITUAL AND THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS OF HUMAN CARING Caring is often described as a spiritual act, grounded in the nurse's inner values and sense of purpose. Watson's theory offers a robust theoretical foundation for understanding this dimension. Watson's carative factors—now referred to as caritas processes—highlight the importance of cultivating loving-kindness, creating healing environments, and promoting the wholeness of patients.6 Florence Nightingale's work also reflects the spiritual aspect of caring. Nightingale believed that nursing was a sacred calling, emphasizing the connection between health, spirituality, and the environment.2 This holistic perspective continues to inspire nurses to view their work as a means of both addressing physical ailments and nurturing humanity. THE SPECIFIC CALL OF NURSES TO LIVE AND EXPRESS CARING Nurses maintain a unique position in healthcare as both caregivers and advocates. They're often the closest healthcare professionals to patients, providing medical care and emotional support. In fact, nursing is peculiar in its interface with the patient's health journey, not just the events and interventions on a journey gone wrong. This proximity gives nurses a particular call to live and express caring as a core element of their practice. Living out this call involves integrating caring into every interaction, from person-centered care to policy advocacy. For nurses, expressing caring means going beyond tasks and procedures to form meaningful connections. Caring involves seeing the people behind the patients and treating them with respect and empathy as they experience their health journeys. Nurses must also be aware of their own emotional and spiritual needs, because self-care is essential to sustaining the capacity to care for others.7 Caring isn't limited to individual interactions; it also extends to systemic efforts. Nurses are called to advocate for compassionate care and the health policies that support that care and to create work environments that prioritize well-being and healthcare systems that value human dignity. By embodying these principles, nurses fulfill their professional commitment to serve the greater good. CARING IN TODAY'S HUMAN-TECH HEALTHCARE ENVIRONMENT Let's be honest: technology has transformed healthcare. From electronic health records (EHRs) to digital health tools to diagnostic procedures powered by artificial intelligence, technology plays an essential role in improving efficiency and outcomes. But it also presents challenges to the nurse-patient relationship. It's easy to get so caught up in charting or managing the myriad treatment devices that we lose sight of the patient as a person. Surviving and thriving in a healthcare system increasingly focused on revenue, efficiency, hierarchy, and control requires intentional strategies from both nursing leadership and practicing nurses. Nursing leaders must advocate for systems and policies that prioritize human connection. For example, nurse leaders can ensure that staffing and assignment allow for meaningful patient interactions. Leaders should also invest in training programs that emphasize emotional intelligence and relational skills, ensuring that nurses feel equipped to balance efficiency with empathy. Practicing nurses can champion the spirit of caring in their daily work by focusing on the small moments that make a big difference. Even in high-pressure environments, a kind word, a moment of genuine listening, or a compassionate touch can remind patients and their families that the patients are more than their diagnoses. Nurses can also collaborate to create peer-support networks, fostering a culture of care that extends beyond patient interactions to include mutual respect, colleagueship, and encouragement among colleagues. Appreciative leadership emphasizes that innovative leadership is key to preserving caring in hierarchical and financially driven systems.8 It advocates for complex adaptive leadership approaches that empower nurses at all levels to express their ownership and accountability for their professional work and positively transform their work environment.9 By decentralizing decision-making and valuing the ownership of practice by frontline nurses, leaders can create a sense of accountability and commitment to the ethos of caring. Technology, although often seen as a barrier to caring, can also be leveraged to support it.10 For instance, EHRs can be streamlined to reduce administrative tasks, giving nurses more time to focus on direct patient care. Telehealth platforms can extend access to underserved populations, allowing nurses to demonstrate caring through education and ongoing support in virtual settings. ADVOCACY FOR CARING Nursing advocacy for caring must go beyond traditional approaches and embrace bold, innovative efforts that challenge the status quo. At the leadership level, advocacy can include pushing for policies that, in real time, can balance workload and scheduling to provide nurses with the time needed for meaningful interactions. Leaders can also advocate for caring-centered metrics in healthcare evaluation systems, ensuring that compassion and patient interaction and satisfaction are valued alongside financial performance. In healthcare settings, out-of-the-box advocacy might include creating dedicated caring forums where nurses, patients, and families collaborate to develop initiatives that promote empathy and human connection. For example, implementing programs that allow nurses to participate in regular mindfulness or reflective practices can enhance their ability to stay grounded and connected with patients. In policy efforts, nurses can work toward legislation that protects and enhances the caring aspects of healthcare. For example, advocating for state or federal laws that fund training programs focused on relational and emotional intelligence in healthcare professionals can create systemic change. Policymakers could also be lobbied to support grants for community outreach programs that emphasize holistic, patient-centered care. Nurses could even become members of these decision-making bodies. Within nursing professional governance, bold advocacy could involve restructuring nursing leadership models to elevate the voice and decision-making role of practicing nurses. By creating avenues for direct participation in organizational decision-making, nurses can verify that policies align with the core values of nursing. Professional governance in organizations could establish awards or recognition for nurses who exemplify extraordinary care and demonstrate its impact, spotlighting the importance of this foundational nursing quality. On an individual level, practicing nurses can take brave steps to advocate for caring by mentoring new nurses in compassionate practices, sharing stories of impactful patient interactions in professional forums, and speaking up when institutional priorities conflict with caring values. Additionally, individual nurses might volunteer in community health initiatives or collaborate with interdisciplinary teams to address social determinants of health, demonstrating caring beyond the hospital walls. These collective efforts, both large and small, can help ensure that the centrality of caring thrives even in challenging and complex healthcare environments. WHY CARING MUST STAY CENTRAL IN A DIGITAL FUTURE Caring isn't just a nice idea; it's essential for effective healthcare. Studies show that compassionate care has an impact on the patient experience and positive healing outcomes.11 Beyond measurable outcomes, caring is what distinguishes nursing as a profession centered on the holistic well-being of individuals, not just their medical conditions. In a digital future, the expression of caring may need to adapt to incorporate new tools and environments. Virtual care platforms, for instance, require nurses to build rapport and empathy through screens. This process might involve developing a heightened sensitivity to verbal cues, body language, and even the tone of written communication. Additionally, nurses can use technology to augment their caring practices by leveraging data to anticipate needs, personalize care plans, and improve patient education. Another way caring might evolve is through greater use of interdisciplinary collaboration supported by digital tools. Nurses will likely spend more time coordinating care using advanced data systems, making it crucial to maintain the human touch in these interactions. Quantum leadership's emphasis on innovative leadership is particularly relevant here, arguing that nurses must advocate for systems that prioritize patient relationships even as they integrate technology.12 For future nurses, in the face of contemporary political crosscurrents, expressing caring will also mean embracing cultural competence and equity in increasingly diverse and globalized healthcare systems. Technology can support cultural competency by offering resources for language translation, cultural education, and tailored care strategies. However, the responsibility remains with the nurse to ensure that these tools are used in ways that deepen understanding and connection, rather than creating distance and polarization. Ultimately, the centrality of caring in nursing dictates that no matter how advanced our tools become, the essence of nursing—human connection and empathy—is preserved. The challenge for future nurses will be to seamlessly integrate these new expressions of caring into their practice without compromising the integrity of the nurse-patient relationship. A LEGACY OF CARING Nursing has a proud history of caring, and it's up to each of us to ensure this legacy continues. By drawing on the wisdom of pioneers like Nightingale, Barton, Mahoney, Wald, Watson, and many others, we can navigate the challenges of today's healthcare environment without losing sight of what makes nursing unique. Caring isn't just part of our work, caring is the heart of the nursing profession. Let's reaffirm this commitment and inspire the next generation of nurses to carry it forward.
